steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Anomaly detection is the task of finding unusual instances. There are two issues that hinder performance: how to get a "good" representation of the normal data, and not knowing the nature of the anomalies. Self-supervised learning techniques have mainly addressed these issues in complex domains like computer vision and natural language processing. But these techniques have not given the same benefits for tabular data.

Self-supervised learning usually uses a pretext task to learn the intrinsic structure of the training data. Examples of pretext tasks are colourising greyscale images or predicting the next word in a sentence. If you understand the typical characteristics of a domain, you can choose an effective pretext task. For example, colourisation needs knowledge of object boundaries and semantics, and these are useful for image classification. But for images or text, spatial or sequential biases are natural starting points for self-supervision, while for tabular data the starting points are not clear.

A recent study showed that self-supervised learning does not help tabular anomaly detection. Reiss et al. compared two self-supervised methods with k -nearest neighbours (k -NN) on the original features. The methods were designed for tabular data, but still k -NN on the original features worked the best.

- Our investigation
  - why?; more comprehensive suite of pretext tasks; synthetic test cases; analyse learnt representations
  - self-supervision doesn't improve; deep nets introduce redundant features -> detectors less effective
  - recover performance using subspace of network's representation
  - self-supervision better for purely localised anomalies and different dependency structures
  - also benchmark: no anomalies during training; complement + practical insight on which detectors work better
- Contributions
  - 1. reconfirm ineffectiveness
  - 2. investigate why empirically
  - 3. comprehensive one-class benchmark with several self-supervised methods
  - 4. practical insights, when detectors/pretext tasks help
- Outline: Section 2 setup; Section 3 experimental approach; Section 4 evaluation; Section 5 summary/conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Anomaly detection is the task of finding unusual instances. There are two issues that hinder performance: how to get a "good" representation of the normal data, and not knowing the nature of the anomalies. Self-supervised learning techniques have mainly addressed these issues in complex domains like computer vision and natural language processing. But these techniques have not given the same benefits for tabular data.

Self-supervised learning usually uses a pretext task to learn the intrinsic structure of the training data. Examples of pretext tasks are colourising greyscale images or predicting the next word in a sentence. If you understand the typical characteristics of a domain, you can choose an effective pretext task. For example, colourisation needs knowledge of object boundaries and semantics, and these are useful for image classification. But for images or text, spatial or sequential biases are natural starting points for self-supervision, while for tabular data the starting points are not clear.

A recent study showed that self-supervised learning does not help tabular anomaly detection. Reiss et al. compared two self-supervised methods with k -nearest neighbours (k -NN) on the original features. The methods were designed for tabular data, but still k -NN on the original features worked the best.

We want to understand why this happens. We extend the experiments with a more comprehensive suite of pretext tasks. We also add synthetic test cases and we analyse the learnt representations underneath. Our results confirm again that self-supervision does not improve tabular anomaly detection performance, and they indicate that deep neural networks introduce redundant features, which makes anomaly detectors less effective. On the other hand, we can recover performance by using a subspace of the neural network's representation. We also show that self-supervised learning can do better than the original representation for purely localised anomalies and for anomalies with different dependency structures.

Besides these investigations, we also ran a series of experiments to benchmark anomaly detection performance in a setting where we do not have access to anomalies during training. We include these findings to complement the self-supervision results and to give practical insight into scenarios where specific detectors work better than others.

Our contributions are:

- 1. We confirm again that self-supervision is ineffective for tabular anomaly detection.

- 2. We investigate empirically why self-supervision does not help tabular anomaly detection.

- 3. We introduce a comprehensive one-class anomaly detection benchmark with several self-supervised methods.

- 4. We give practical insights and find cases where particular anomaly detectors and pretext tasks may help.

Section 2 covers the anomaly detection setup. Section 3 outlines our experimental approach. Section 4 evaluates our findings. Section 5 summarises our work and concludes.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Anomaly detection is the task of identifying unusual instances. Two issues hinder performance: how to obtain a "good" representation of the normal data, and a lack of knowledge about the nature of anomalies. The emergence of self-supervised learning techniques has primarily addressed these issues in complex domains such as computer vision and natural language processing [1,2]. However, these techniques have not yielded the same benefits for tabular data [3].

Self-supervised learning typically uses a pretext task to learn the intrinsic structure of the training data [4]. Examples of pretext tasks include colourising greyscale images [5] or predicting the next word in a sentence [6,7]. Understanding the typical characteristics of a domain allows one to choose an effective pretext task. For instance, colourisation requires knowledge of object boundaries and semantics, which are useful for image classification [8,9]. However, unlike images or text, where spatial or sequential biases are natural starting points for self-supervision, the starting points for tabular data are unclear.

A recent study indicated that self-supervised learning does not help tabular anomaly detection [3]. Reiss et al. compared two self-supervised methods with k -nearest neighbours (k -NN) on the original features. Even though the methods were designed for tabular data, they found that k -NN on the original features worked best.

We seek to understand why this is the case. We extend the experiments to include a more comprehensive suite of pretext tasks, incorporate synthetic test cases, and analyse the underlying learnt representations. Our results reinforce that self-supervision does not improve tabular anomaly detection performance, and indicate that deep neural networks introduce redundant features, which reduces the effectiveness of anomaly detectors. Conversely, we can recover performance using a subspace of the neural network's representation. We also show that self-supervised learning can outperform the original representation in the case of purely localised anomalies and those with different dependency structures.

In addition, we ran a series of experiments to benchmark anomaly detection performance in a setting where we do not have access to anomalies during training. We include these findings as a complement to the self-supervision results and to provide practical insight into scenarios where specific detectors work better than others.

Our contributions are as follows:

- 1. We reconfirm the ineffectiveness of self-supervision for tabular anomaly detection.

- 2. We empirically investigate why self-supervision does not benefit tabular anomaly detection.

- 3. We introduce a comprehensive one-class anomaly detection benchmark using several self-supervised methods.

- 4. We provide practical insights and identify instances where particular anomaly detectors and pretext tasks may be beneficial.

In Section 2, we cover the anomaly detection setup. We then outline our experimental approach in Section 3 and evaluate our findings in Section 4. Finally, we summarise our work and conclude in Section 5.
